node.title: Human Health and Disease: Introduction about health; Common diseases in humans

questions.stem: Ascariasis, an intestinal disease of humans, is caused by
questions.explanation: Ascariasis is caused by the intestinal roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. Its eggs leave the body in the faeces of an infected person and contaminate soil, water and plants, and a healthy person is infected by taking in these eggs. Symptoms include internal bleeding, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage.

optionRationale.2: Wuchereria bancrofti is the filarial worm that causes filariasis.
optionRationale.3: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan that causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery).
optionRationale.4: Trichophyton is a fungus that is one of the causes of ringworm.

questions.stem: Ringworms, which cause dry scaly lesions on the skin, nails and scalp, are caused by
questions.explanation: Ringworm is a fungal infection caused by fungi of the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. Heat and moisture help these fungi to grow, so the lesions appear in skin folds such as the groin and between the toes. It spreads by sharing towels, clothes or combs.

optionRationale.1: Typhoid and pneumonia are bacterial, but ringworm is not.
optionRationale.3: Common cold is viral, but ringworm is not a viral disease.
optionRationale.4: Malaria and amoebiasis are protozoan diseases, not ringworm.

questions.stem: The common cold, which affects the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs, is caused by
questions.explanation: The common cold is caused by rhinoviruses, which infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs. It is spread by droplets from coughs and sneezes or by contaminated objects. Pneumonia, in contrast, is caused by bacteria that infect the alveoli of the lungs.

optionRationale.1: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterial cause of pneumonia, not the cold.
optionRationale.2: Haemophilus influenzae is another bacterial cause of pneumonia, not the cold.
optionRationale.4: Salmonella typhi is the bacterium that causes typhoid fever.

questions.objective: State the cause of the common cold

questions.stem: Heroin, commonly called smack, is chemically
options: morphine taken directly from the latex of the poppy
a cannabinoid from the hemp plant
an alkaloid obtained from the coca plant
diacetylmorphine, made by acetylation of morphine
questions.explanation: Heroin is diacetylmorphine, a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is itself extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum. It is taken by snorting or injection and acts as a depressant that slows body functions.

optionRationale.1: Morphine is the starting material, but heroin is made from it by chemical modification.
optionRationale.2: Cannabinoids come from Cannabis sativa and are a different group of drugs.
optionRationale.3: The coca plant gives cocaine, not heroin.

questions.objective: Recall the chemical nature of heroin

questions.stem: The spread of cancerous cells from the primary tumour through blood to distant sites of the body is called
questions.explanation: Neoplastic cells from a malignant tumour may enter the blood or lymph and reach other places, where they start new tumours. This spreading to distant sites is called metastasis, and it is the most dangerous property of malignant tumours, since benign tumours remain confined to their site of origin.

optionRationale.1: Neoplasia is the uncontrolled new growth of cells that forms the tumour, not their spread.
optionRationale.3: Malignancy describes a tumour that can invade and spread, not the act of spreading itself.
optionRationale.4: Carcinogenesis is the process by which normal cells become cancerous.

questions.stem: Which technique uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation to detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue?
questions.explanation: Magnetic resonance imaging uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation to detect changes in living tissue, including cancerous ones. A biopsy involves examining a thin tissue section under a microscope, while radiography and computed tomography use X-rays.

optionRationale.1: Biopsy is the microscopic study of a thin slice of tissue, not a magnetic technique.
optionRationale.3: Computed tomography uses X-rays to build a three-dimensional image, so it is ionising.

questions.objective: Identify an imaging technique used for cancer detection

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about allergy and autoimmunity.
A. Allergy is an exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens called allergens.
B. During an allergic reaction, histamine and serotonin are released from mast cells.
C. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
D. Allergy is caused by bacterial pathogens that invade the blood.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Allergy is an exaggerated response to allergens, with release of histamine and serotonin from mast cells, and rheumatoid arthritis arises when the body attacks its own cells, so A, B and C are correct. Allergens are harmless substances like dust and pollen, not invading bacteria, so D is wrong.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: Statement A is also correct, so this is incomplete.
optionRationale.4: Statement D is false; allergens are generally harmless environmental substances such as pollen and dust mites.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on allergy and autoimmunity

questions.stem: Match List-I (disease) with List-II (mode of spread or vector) and choose the correct code.

right: I. Bite of the female Culex mosquito
II. Bite of the female Anopheles mosquito
III. Houseflies acting as mechanical carriers
IV. Soil, water and plants contaminated with eggs from faeces

questions.explanation: Malaria is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito (A-II). Filariasis, caused by filarial worms, is transmitted by the female Culex mosquito (B-I). In amoebiasis, houseflies act as mechanical carriers of the cysts (C-III), and ascariasis spreads through eggs that contaminate soil, water and plants (D-IV).

optionRationale.2: A and B are interchanged; Anopheles spreads malaria and Culex spreads filariasis.
optionRationale.3: C and D are interchanged; ascaris eggs contaminate soil and plants, while flies carry amoebic cysts.
optionRationale.4: A and C are interchanged; malaria is spread by a mosquito, not by houseflies.

questions.objective: Match diseases with their mode of transmission

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In an HIV-infected person the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the body steadily decreases.
Reason (R): HIV is a retrovirus with an RNA genome.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes, replicates in them and destroys them, so their numbers fall and the person becomes immune-deficient. HIV is indeed a retrovirus with an RNA genome, but that fact only describes the virus and does not by itself explain why helper T cells are lost.

optionRationale.1: Having an RNA genome does not explain the fall in T-cells; the loss is due to the virus replicating in and destroying these cells.
optionRationale.3: R is true; HIV is a retrovirus whose genome is RNA.
optionRationale.4: A is true; falling helper T-cell numbers is the hallmark of AIDS.

questions.objective: Relate HIV infection to loss of helper T cells

questions.stem: Which of the following is a physiological barrier of innate immunity?
options: Mucus coating of the respiratory tract
questions.explanation: Innate immunity has four types of barriers. Gastric acid, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes are physiological barriers that prevent microbial growth. Skin and mucus are physical barriers, and macrophages and neutrophils are cellular barriers.

optionRationale.1: Skin is the main physical barrier.
optionRationale.2: Mucus trapping microbes in the respiratory tract is a physical barrier.
optionRationale.4: Macrophages are phagocytic cells and belong to the cellular barriers.

questions.stem: In the life cycle of Plasmodium, the gametocytes are formed in human red blood cells. They develop further, and fertilisation occurs, in the
options: gut of the female Anopheles mosquito
questions.explanation: When a female Anopheles bites an infected person it takes up the gametocytes with the blood. Fertilisation takes place in the mosquito gut and the zygote develops into sporozoites, which move to the salivary glands. These sporozoites are the infective stage injected into the next human host.

optionRationale.1: The mosquito has no liver stage; the liver stage occurs in the human host.
optionRationale.2: Humans have no salivary stage; the sporozoites collect in the salivary glands of the mosquito.
optionRationale.3: The sexual stage of Plasmodium is completed in the mosquito, not in the human stomach.

questions.objective: Locate the sexual phase of Plasmodium

questions.stem: A person exposed for the second time to the same antigen mounts a quicker and stronger response. This is mainly due to
questions.explanation: During the first encounter, B and T lymphocytes produce memory cells that persist in the body. On the second exposure the memory cells recognise the antigen at once and respond rapidly with a much larger antibody production. Innate cells such as NK cells and neutrophils respond the same way each time.

optionRationale.2: NK cells are part of innate immunity, which has no memory.
optionRationale.3: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes whose response does not improve on repeated exposure.
optionRationale.4: Interferons are non-specific antiviral proteins and do not give immunological memory.

questions.objective: Attribute the secondary response to memory cells

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. Oncogenic transformation of normal cells can be caused by physical, chemical or biological agents.
B. Cancer cells grow rapidly and invade neighbouring tissues.
C. ELISA, based on the antigen-antibody reaction, is used for diagnosis of AIDS.
D. All forms of cancer are caused by viruses.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Carcinogens may be physical (X-rays, gamma rays), chemical (tobacco smoke) or biological (oncogenic viruses), so A is right. Cancer cells divide uncontrollably and invade nearby tissues, so B is right, and ELISA is used to diagnose HIV infection, so C is right. Cancer has many causes, not only viruses, so D is wrong.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this misses it.
optionRationale.3: Statement D is false, and statement A is left out.
optionRationale.4: Statement D is false, and statement B is left out.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on cancer and AIDS diagnosis

questions.stem: Opioid drugs such as morphine produce their effects by binding to specific opioid receptors present in the
options: central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract
questions.explanation: Opioids bind to specific opioid receptors present in the central nervous system and the gastrointestinal tract. Their binding explains the pain relief and sedation that morphine produces, and also its depressant action on the body. Cannabinoids act on receptors in the brain, and are different from opioids.

optionRationale.1: Opioid receptors are not found mainly in the heart and kidneys.
optionRationale.2: The liver and lungs are not the sites of the main opioid receptors.
optionRationale.4: Opioid receptors are not located mainly in skeletal muscle or bone.

questions.objective: Recall the site of action of opioids

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A benign tumour is generally less dangerous than a malignant tumour.
Reason (R): Benign tumours remain confined to the place of origin and cause little damage, while malignant tumour cells can spread to other sites.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Benign tumours stay at their site and rarely cause much damage, whereas malignant tumours invade tissues and metastasise to distant sites, which makes them life-threatening. This difference in spread directly explains why benign tumours are the less dangerous kind.

optionRationale.2: R is not a separate fact; the confinement versus spread is exactly why one is less dangerous.
optionRationale.3: R is true; benign tumours stay confined and malignant cells can metastasise.
optionRationale.4: A is true; benign tumours are usually less harmful.
